column2: Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, desire and anger, being and non-being, killing, bondage and release: all is obtained through Time.
I am not the doer, nor are you; the doer is the one who is always lord; this Time cooks me like a fruit come to the tree.
Whatever a man does, by which he is joined with pleasures by Time, doing those same things he is again joined with pains by Time.
One who knows Time, touched by Time, has no need to grieve; therefore, Shakra, I do not grieve; there is no help in grief.
Since for those who grieve, grief does not remove calamity, and the grieving have no power, therefore I do not grieve today."
Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed blessed Shatakratu, Pakashasana, drew back his fury and said:

Seeing the arm raised with the thunderbolt and the snares of Varuna, whose mind would not tremble, even before one wishing to kill, even Death?
mahabharata:12:220.90	That mind of yours does not tremble, unmoving, seeing the truth; speaking, you do not tremble, you of true valour.
mahabharata:12:220.91	Who, an embodied one, would venture trust in affairs or in the body in the world, seeing the world departing?
mahabharata:12:220.92	I too know this world as thus eternal, placed in the fire of Time, dreadful, secret, ever moving, imperishable.
mahabharata:12:220.93	Here there is no escape for anyone touched by Time, for beings subtle and great being cooked.
mahabharata:12:220.94	For one who has no master, who is unheedful, who ever cooks beings, who does not turn back, Time: one who has come to destruction is not freed.
mahabharata:12:220.95	Time is watchful among the heedless, among the embodied; it has not been seen by anyone to be overcome, even by effort.
mahabharata:12:220.96	It is the ancient eternal dharma, equal to all who bear breath; Time cannot be avoided, and its course cannot be transgressed.
mahabharata:12:220.97	Time kneads together our days and nights, months, moments, kashthas, kalas and lavas, like a moneylender his hoard of understanding.
mahabharata:12:220.98	Of the man who says, I shall do this today, I shall do it tomorrow," Time takes him when it comes, as a river's current a raft.
Only just now I saw him; how has he died? Such lament of men is heard as Time carries them off.
Wealth and enjoyments perish, and place and lordship; all is impermanent and unsteady; resolve is hard; heights end in falls; being and non-being stand together.
That mind of yours does not tremble, unmoving, seeing truth; you do not even think in mind, "I was so before."
When this world is overpowered and cooked by mighty Time, you are not aware of being cast down, with no eldest and no youngest.
The world, attached to envy, conceit and greed, to desire, anger and fear, to longing, delusion and pride, is bewildered.
But you, a knower of the truth of states, learned, endowed with knowledge and austerity, see Time clearly like an amalaka fruit in the hand.
Knowing the truth of Time's course, versed in all the scriptures, son of Virochana, you are self-trained and to be desired by the wise.
I think the whole world has been grasped by your intellect; roaming, freed on every side, you cling nowhere.
Neither rajas nor tamas touch you, master of senses; without craving, your torment gone, you resort to the self.
Seeing you, a friend of all beings, without enmity, of tranquil mind, a compassionate thought toward you has arisen in me.
I do not wish to kill such an understanding in bondage; non-cruelty is the highest dharma, and mercy toward you.
These snares of Varuna will be loosened, by the turn of time, by the misconduct of the people; good luck to you, great asura.
When the daughter-in-law will employ her old mother-in-law in service, and the son will send his father to tasks through delusion,
when shudras will make brahmanas wash their feet, and shudras will approach brahmana wives fearlessly,
when men will sow seeds in wrong wombs, mixing, and offer oblations with bronze vessels and bad utensils,
when the whole fourfold order will be without limit, then one by one your snares will be loosened.
You have no fear from me; keep to the agreement; be happy, unhindered, with tranquil mind and free of disease."
Having so spoken to him, the blessed Shatakratu, mounted on the king of elephants, went off; having conquered all the asuras, the lord of the gods rejoiced with delight and became sole king.
The great sages praised him readily, Vrishakapi, lord of all the moving and unmoving; the removers of cold carried the offering quickly, and nectar was offered to the lord.
Praised by the best of the twice-born everywhere, blazing with radiance, free of anger, the lord, calm of mind and glad, reached his own abode in heaven, and Vasava rejoiced.
[Bhishma said:] "The mind alone of a man announces his future shapes, what is auspicious to him and what is not to be.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Shri with Shakra; learn it, Yudhishthira.
Seeing the higher and lower worlds by the dawn of great austerity, having gone, as common to the sages dwelling in Brahma's world,
Narada himself, of immeasurable radiance, his sin calmed, of great austerity, roamed at will in the three worlds.
Once, rising in the morning, wishing to touch pure water, he went to the Ganga with its gate at Dhruva, and descended.
And the thousand-eyed wielder of the thunderbolt, slayer of Shambara and Paka, came to the bank of that river frequented by divine sages.
Having bathed, the two self-controlled ones sat reciting prayers, having reached the river's sandbank of fine golden sand.
Those two, fond of tales, pure and glad in mind, told stories told by divine sages and related by those of holy deeds, attentive, speaking of things free of past events.
Then, Bharata, there appeared coming near them the course of the Garuda and the sun, the Vaishnava path, shining unequalled with brightness, illuminating the three worlds.
Preceded by apsarases of divine form and beauty, tall, with the radiance of the great sun's rays,
with ornaments like stars and a garland like rows of stars, they saw Shri, Padma, standing in person on a lotus.
She, best of women, descending from the front of her aerial car, approached the lord of the three worlds, Shakra, and the sage Narada.
Followed by Narada, Maghavan came to the goddess in person, with folded hands, presenting himself.
And he, all-knowing king of the gods, paid her incomparable honour, and Shri, king, spoke these words.
Who are you, and for what purpose have you come, fair-smiling one? From where do you come, fair-browed, and where are you to go, auspicious one?
[Shri said:] "In the three holy worlds all, moving and unmoving, strive with the highest effort to win my nature.
I am born in a lotus awakened by the sun's rays, for the prosperity of all beings: Padma, Shri, wearing a lotus garland.
I am Lakshmi, I am Bhuti, I am Shri, slayer of Bala; I am faith and intelligence, humility, victory and stability.
I am steadiness, success, splendour and prosperity; I am Svaha, Svadha, praise, destiny and doing.
I dwell at the front of the armies and on the banners of kings who win, in the dwellings of those devoted to dharma, in regions and cities,
in the brave who is victorious, who does not turn back in battle; I dwell in a king of men always, slayer of Bala.
In one constant in dharma, of great wisdom, devoted to brahmanas, truthful, humble and generous, I always dwell.
Formerly I lived among the asuras, bound to truth and dharma; knowing them as reversed, I chose to dwell in you."
[Shakra said:] "How did you dwell among the Daityas when they behaved so, fair-faced one? And seeing what, have you left the Daityas and Danavas and come here?"
[Shri said:] "I was devoted to beings who followed their own dharma, unmoved through steadiness, delighting in the path to heaven.
Among them giving, study, sacrifice, honouring teachers and deities, and brahmans and guests went on constantly.
Their houses were well swept, their women controlled, the fires fed; they served their teachers, were self-controlled, devoted to brahmanas and truthful.
Faithful, conquerors of anger, generous, without envy, they maintained sons, ministers and wives, and were free of jealousy.
Not intolerant, they never craved each other's things, and the steadfast were never tormented by others' prosperity.
They were givers, gatherers, noble, knowers of compassion, of great kindness, honest, firm in devotion, masters of senses.
They had contented servants and ministers, were grateful, kind in speech, and gave wealth and honour as due, modest, of fixed vows.
Always well bathed at the festivals, well anointed, well adorned, given to fasting and austerity, famed speakers of Brahman.
The sun did not rise on them, nor did they sleep at dawn; at night they always avoided curds and barley-meal.
Pure celibate students looked each morning at ghee, saw auspicious things and honoured brahmanas.
Dharma ever belongs to those who give, ever to those who do not take, to those who sleep half the night and do not sleep by day.
They ever approved of inheritance and share for the wretched, the helpless, the aged, the weak, the sick and women.
They ever comforted the despondent, the frightened, the agitated, the fear-stricken, the sick, the robbed and the afflicted by calamity.
They followed dharma alone and did not harm each other; they were agreeable in tasks and served elders.
They properly honoured ancestors, gods and guests, and ate the remains, ever devoted to truth and austerity.
They did not eat alone when well provided, did not go to another's wife, and behaved toward all beings with compassion as toward themselves.
Neither by day, nor with animals, nor in a wrong womb, nor on festival days did they ever care to release the senses.
Ever giving, skilled, honest, ever energetic and without ego, of highest friendship and forbearance,
truth, giving, austerity, purity, compassion, unharsh speech, no treachery to friends: all this was in them, lord.
Sleep, drowsiness, passion, envy, disregard, discontent and despondency and longing did not enter them.
I dwelt long ago among such Danavas, from the creation of beings through more than one reversal of the ages.
Then, in the reversal of time, by the reversal of their qualities, I saw dharma gone from those under the sway of desire and anger.
In assemblies of the aged, those of lesser virtue laughed at and envied all the elders who told true tales.
They no longer honoured as before the good aged who came to sit with the young, with rising and salutation.
Sons, becoming masters, treated their fathers as enemy servants, proclaiming it, shameless.
They hankered after the great wealth gained by deeds blamed and apart from dharma.
They spoke loudly at night while the fire burned low; sons spoke back to fathers and wives to husbands.
They did not honour mother, father, aged teacher, guest or elder, and did not look after the young.
Without giving alms or offerings, they ate food themselves, without sacrifice, not sharing with ancestors, gods, guests and elders.
They did not care about purity; their cooks too; in mind, deed and word there was uncovered fault.
Grain lay scattered, food for crows and mice; milk stood uncovered; they touched ghee while unclean.
Spades and spittoons, scattered bronze vessels, and all the household utensils the housewife did not look to.
They did not repair the ruin of walls and houses, and did not regard animals, tying them up with fodder and water.
The Danavas ate their own food while children looked on, and gave only leavings to all their servants.
They cooked milk-rice, sesame rice, meat, cakes and fried cakes for themselves, and ate meat in vain.
They slept after sunrise and woke at dawn; quarrels went on day and night in house after house.
The ignoble sat attending an elder; there, those out of their stages, doing wrong deeds, hated one another; mixing arose, and purity did not remain.
Brahmanas who knew the Veda and those who clearly did not were without difference; they were bound up in honour and dishonour.
Servants took up a bad practice of looking at fashion, ornaments, dress, gait and stance.
Women in the dress of men and men in the dress of women found great delight in play and pleasure walks.
What had been given in the past by the wealthy to the worthy, they did not follow, from unbelief, though living in plenty.
A friend, asked for help by a friend when the wealth was in doubt, destroyed that wealth for his own purpose, for a mere tip of a thing.
Fond of taking others' goods, dealing in markets, they were seen among the noble classes; and even shudras were rich in austerity.
Some studied without keeping vows, others kept vows in vain; a disciple did not serve his teacher, a teacher became his disciple's friend.
Father and mother, wearied, were as if at a festival of conduct, powerless, and asked their sons for food in vain.
There the Veda-knowing wise, deep like the ocean, became attached to farming and the like; fools ate at shraddhas.
The good questions each morning, preparation, sending, and tasks were done by disciples sent by teachers.
A daughter-in-law commanded servants in front of her father- and mother-in-law, and, calling her husband, addressed him.
A father, though he guarded his son's mind with effort, shared in anger and lived in sorrow.
Seeing wealth taken by fire, thieves or kings, they laughed from hatred, even those esteemed as friends.
The ungrateful, unbelieving, sinful, violators of the teacher's wife, delighting in eating forbidden food, without limit, their lustre gone.
When they were practising such conduct in reversal, I thought: I shall not dwell among the Danavas, lord of the gods.
Welcome me, who have come of myself to you, lord of Shachi; honoured by you, lord of the gods, the gods will set me in front.
Where I am, there are my beloved, more excellent, devoted to me, seven goddesses and eight with me; they will bring my wealth.
Hope, faith, steadiness, beauty, victory, humility, forbearance, and eighth livelihood: these are led by me, Pakashasana.
Those and I, leaving the asuras, have come to your realm; we shall dwell among the thirty gods whose selves are devoted to dharma."

In a pure, honoured place the gods stood in numbers, wishing to see Maghavan seated with Lakshmi.
Then the thousand-eyed one, bull of the gods, reaching heaven with Shri and his friend the divine sage, went in the chariot with bay horses, honoured, to the assembly of the gods.

Then Narada, pondering in mind the intent of the thunderbolt-bearer and of the goddess Shri, who had seen the manliness of the immortal, told Shri of the auspicious and greatly prospering arrival there.
Then radiant heaven rained nectar in the house of the self-born Grandfather; unstruck drums sounded, and the quarters shone clear.
Vasava rained on the crops in season; no one strayed from the path of dharma; the earth was adorned with many mines of jewels; sounds of victory arose for those who dwelt on earth.
Men delighting in action became renowned, standing in the auspicious path of the virtuous; men, gods, kinnaras, yakshas and rakshasas were prosperous, happy and famous.
Never was a flower out of season, much less fruit; none fell from a tree even when blown by wind; cows gave the juice of wishes; no harsh speech passed anyone's lips.
Those who read this worship, with all who grant desires, and Shri, and the gods led by Shakra, in a meeting of brahmins, with prosperity of desires gain fortune.

Asita Devala said to the greatly wise Jaigishavya, who knew the entire tradition of the dharmas, not angry, not glad:
You are not pleased when honoured, nor angry when blamed; what is your wisdom, whence is it, and what is its end?
Thus questioned by him, the great ascetic answered him with great, unambiguous, pure words, with the sense of the lotus.

The goal, the supreme end, the peace of those of meritorious deeds: that I shall tell you, since you ask me, twice-born.

mahabharata:12:222.13	Free of envy, they never harm each other, and the steadfast are never tormented by others' prosperity.
mahabharata:12:222.14	They who do not speak overmuch in blame or praise of others, and are never altered by blame or praise,

mahabharata:12:222.19	Men follow whatever path they wish; by blame or praise there will be no loss or gain for me.

[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you, bull of the Bharatas, as you ask, the dialogue of Ugrasena and Keshava about Narada.
[Ugrasena said:] "See, the world is stirred at the mention of Narada; I think he is endowed with virtues; tell me, as I ask."
[Vasudeva said:] "Hear from me, lord of the Kukuras, as I wish to tell, the good virtues of Narada in brief, lord of men.
His pride does not arise from conduct and destroy the body; his learning and conduct are unbroken; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Narada is truly an ascetic; there is no transgression in his speech, whether from desire or greed; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Knower of the truth of the rule of the self, patient, capable, master of his senses, honest and truthful, therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Great in energy, fame, intellect, policy, humility, birth and austerity; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Easy in nature, a good companion, a good eater, of good manners, pure, of good speech and free of envy; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
He truly does good; there is no sin in him; he is not pleased by others' misfortunes; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
He seeks aims through Vedic hearing and tales, is patient and not contemptuous; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Through equanimity none is dear or undear to him; he speaks in agreement with the mind; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Much learned, a teller of tales, wise, tireless, not crooked, undismayed, not angry and not greedy; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Never has he had a quarrel over wealth, dharma or desire; his faults are cut off; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Firm in devotion, blameless in self, learned, merciful, free of delusion and fault; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Unattached to all attachments, yet seeming attached, not long in doubt, eloquent; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
He does not concentrate for honour, never praises himself, is free of envy and firm in speech; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Not reproaching the world's varied conduct or nature, skilled in the science of association; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
He envies no tradition, does not live on his austerity, never wastes time, master of himself; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Of toil done, of trained wisdom, never satiated in concentration, steady in rules and heedful; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Modest and disciplined, easily led by others toward the good, not betraying others' secrets; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
He does not rejoice at gains nor suffer at losses, of steady mind and unattached; therefore he is honoured everywhere.
Who would not love one endowed with all virtues, skilled, pure, undaunted, knowing time and policy?"
[Yudhishthira said:] "The truth of the world in full, the coming and going of beings, creation and death: whence does all this proceed?
If you wish to favour us here, best of the good, I ask you this; you should tell it to me.

most righteous, set in a divine arrangement; I ask further; you should tell it."

Having studied all the Vedas with their limbs and Upanishads, and seeking final action from seeing skill in dharma,
Shuka, son of Vyasa, asked Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa about this doubt, with his doubts about dharma and wealth cut:
The maker of the host of beings, the settled knowledge of Time, and what a brahmana's duty is: you should tell me.
Fifteen winks make a kashtha; thirty kashthas one reckons as a kala; thirty kalas make a muhurta, with a tenth part of a kala besides.

Thirty muhurtas make a day and a night, as the sages have counted; a month is thirty days and nights; the year is said to have twelve months; those who know numbers speak of two courses in the year, south and north.
The sun divides day and night in the human world; night is for beings' sleep and day for the activity of deeds.
A month is a day and night of the ancestors, and the division of them is again: the dark half is day for action, the bright half is night for sleep.
A year is a day and night of the gods, and their division again: the day is the northern course and the night the southern course.
The day and night of the gods which were told before: reckoning them, I shall tell the sum of years at Brahma's day and night.
I shall tell their sums of years in order: in the Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Kali.
They say four thousand years is the Krita age; its dawn is as many hundreds, and its twilight likewise.
In the other three with their dawns and twilights, thousands and hundreds are reduced by one each.
These hold the eternal worlds; this, dear, is known as the eternal Brahman by the knowers of Brahman.
In the Krita age dharma is fourfold and whole, and truth; no one gains by adharma.
In the others, dharma is reduced a quarter at a time by tradition, and adharma grows by theft, falsehood and deceit.
Free of disease, with all aims accomplished, living four hundred years in the Krita, in the Treta and the rest their lifespan is reduced by a quarter each.
We have heard that Vedic disputations decline with each age, as do lifespans and blessings and the fruit of the Veda.
The dharmas of the Krita are one, of the Treta another, of the Dvapara another, and in the Kali they are as if done as far as possible.
Austerity is supreme in the Krita, knowledge in the Treta, sacrifice they say in the Dvapara, and giving alone in the Kali.
The wise know this as twelve thousand called an age; a thousand turns of it is called a day of Brahma.
Night is as many; at its beginning the lord of the universe, at dissolution, entering the self, sleeps and at the end awakes.
They know the day of Brahma as lasting a thousand ages, and the night as ending after a thousand ages; so say those who know day and night.
Awakened, at the end of the night, the imperishable Brahma acts; he creates the great being, and from that the mind of manifest nature.
His semen is made of Brahma's energy, from which all this world; of the one being, being is twofold, moving and unmoving.
Awakened at the beginning of day, he creates the world by knowledge; first of all the great being, swiftly, the mind of manifest nature."
